hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
By your 70s, even vigorous exercise may do little to reverse a stiffened heart.

In a small study from (previous FMF guest) Dr. Ben Levine’s team, sedentary adults around age 70 trained for a year. Their VO2 max rose 19%, but heart stiffness changed little.

Midlife appears to offer a better window. When sedentary adults ages 45–64 completed two years of structured training that included vigorous intervals, their VO2 max rose 18%, and heart stiffness improved.

The heart can still respond to training later in life. But changing its stiffness may require sustained, demanding exercise before those changes become harder to reverse.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Rhonda Patrick on the ageing heart: by your 70s even hard exercise may do little to undo a stiff heart.

In a small study from Dr Ben Levine's team, sedentary people around 70 trained for a year. Their VO2 max went up 19%, but heart stiffness barely changed. People aged 45 to 64 who did two years of structured training with hard intervals got an 18% VO2 max gain and their hearts got less stiff.

So midlife is the window. If you're in your 50s or early 60s, this is the time to get puffed a few times a week, not "one day". Training still helps later, but the earlier you start, the more you keep.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Nearly 99% of new food ingredients haven't received formal FDA approval. And in some cases, the FDA may not even know an ingredient is being used.

It’s called GRAS, or “generally recognized as safe.”

A company can review the evidence and reach its own conclusion that an ingredient’s intended use is safe, all without notifying the FDA.

Think about that when you turn over a package and see a long list of ingredients you don’t recognize. You might assume someone at the FDA has reviewed them. That’s not necessarily the case. In the European Union, food additives must undergo a scientific safety assessment and receive authorization before they can be used. There’s no equivalent self-affirmed GRAS pathway.

This came up in my conversation with Dr. Dariush Mozaffarian in the latest episode of the podcast, and it’s something I think deserves much more attention. He says the FDA has proposed requiring notification for these GRAS uses, but that change isn’t final.

An unfamiliar ingredient name doesn’t automatically mean something is harmful. But we should want to know that someone outside the company selling it has evaluated its safety.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Rhonda Patrick on food additives: nearly 99% of new food ingredients in the US haven't had formal FDA approval.

It's called GRAS, "generally recognised as safe". A company can look at the evidence itself, decide its ingredient is safe and never tell the FDA. In the EU, additives need a scientific safety check first.

She's fair about it: a strange name on the label doesn't mean it's harmful. But next time you flip a packet and can't pronounce half of it, remember nobody outside the company may have checked. The fewer packets, the fewer surprises.
hits.video_tip: 8s: hand turning over a packet, zoom on a long ingredient list; captions "99% never approved" "GRAS" "Fewer packets."

hits.name: Ken D Berry MD

This post is misleading. Sodium nitrite is not "one of the worst" things in food, and it has not been shown to cause cancer, Alzheimer's, or diabetes.

The claim is that nitrite converts into a compound that causes those three diseases. Your mouth already turns nitrate into nitrite all day, and about 80% of the nitrate people eat comes from vegetables, not bacon. If nitrite itself were the poison, vegetables would be the toxin.

On cancer: nobody has shown that the sodium nitrite in bacon causes cancer in people.

On Alzheimer's: no one has shown this in people. That claim comes from animal experiments and theories about nitrosamines, not from evidence in people.

On diabetes: a 2024 review of six observational studies found no association with nitrate, which is most of what people eat, and the pooled type 2 diabetes result was not statistically significant.

hits.name: Ken D Berry MD
hits.text:
The Washington Post says eat dark chocolate every day. Their words: "But in the nutrition world, dark chocolate sits atop a special pedestal."

Two sentences later: "It's not entirely clear why."

They open by warning that sugary treats are linked to heart disease and type 2 diabetes. Then they tell you to eat candy every day.

Bethany Doerfler, a Northwestern Medicine dietitian, tells her patients to eat dessert every day and up to an ounce of dark chocolate daily. Her reason: "there really are some health benefits to it."

Only 6.8% of American adults have optimal metabolic health. Telling this nation to eat candy every day is ridiculous. And look at what the science behind it actually is.

Heart: WaPo's first source pooled 17 small dark chocolate trials, 615 people total. It only measured how much an artery stretched on an ultrasound. Not one heart attack, stroke or death was counted.

Blood pressure: Cochrane pooled short trials of chocolate and cocoa products. Blood pressure dropped about 2 points, in trials that averaged only 9 weeks. The Cochrane authors rated it moderate quality, and the effect got smaller when they dropped trials with authors employed by the candy industry sponsors.

The one big randomized trial, COSMOS, didn't use chocolate bars. It gave 21,442 older adults a cocoa extract capsule, 500 mg of cocoa flavanols a day for over 3 years. The extract was supplied by Mars (the candy company). Its main result: no significant drop in heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular events. WaPo led with a secondary number instead.

Diabetes: WaPo's diabetes study gave nobody chocolate. People filled out food questionnaires about how much chocolate they ate and reported their own diabetes. The authors themselves said randomized trials are needed. That randomized trial already exists. COSMOS tested the same cocoa extract against diabetes in 18,381 people. No reduction. WaPo cited COSMOS for the heart and left the diabetes result out.

Mood: 60 women ate under half an ounce of 78% dark chocolate a day for 8 weeks, and the comparison group ate milk chocolate, not no chocolate. The other study gave 48 people in their 20s an ounce of 85% or 70% dark chocolate a day, or none, for 3 weeks. Only 18 got the 85%, and the 70% dark chocolate group showed no mood change at all.

Gut: that same 48-person chocolate study. They only tested the gut bacteria of the 85% group and the no-chocolate group. Then WaPo admits the gut and mood research is "mixed."

That's the case for daily candy: an artery ultrasound, a 2-point blood pressure blip, a cocoa capsule that failed its main test, a food questionnaire, and a few dozen people eating chocolate for a few weeks.

Dark chocolate is candy. Eat it as a treat if you want. But a nutrition professional should not be recommending it to sick people as medicine!

hits.text:
Low-carb diets and your thyroid: what the data actually show

For years the internet has warned that cutting carbs will “wreck your thyroid.” The claim usually rests on one lab finding: T3 often drops on a ketogenic or low-carb diet. What the studies rarely mention is that TSH stays flat or falls, free T4 holds steady or rises, and people do not develop clinical hypothyroidism.

A 2016 trial in overweight adults with Hashimoto’s tested a low-carbohydrate diet (restricted bread, pasta, fruit, and rice, free of goitrogens) for three weeks. Thyroid antibodies plummeted: antithyroid −40 %, anti-microsomal −57 %, TPO −44 %. The control group’s antibodies went up. 

Thyroid hormones themselves did not change significantly, while weight and BMI dropped.
A 2024 randomized study used MRI (Dixon-T2 imaging) to measure thyroid inflammation in Hashimoto’s patients. After six months on a low-carb diet, thyroid water content fell and both TPOAb and TgAb declined significantly. The normal-diet group showed no improvement.

In people with metabolic syndrome, a 2024 trial of time-restricted eating with or without a low-carb diet improved markers of thyroid function alongside heart-muscle enzymes. Clinical programs tracking hundreds of patients on well-formulated ketogenic diets (including Yancy et al. in type 2 diabetes) have not produced new cases of hypothyroidism. TSH remains stable while T3 adapts downward—exactly the pattern seen in fasting, not thyroid failure.

The T3 drop appears adaptive: when insulin and glucose stay low, the body needs less active thyroid hormone to clear carbohydrate. It is not the same as primary hypothyroidism, which requires a rising TSH plus symptoms.

Well-constructed low-carb eating does not damage the thyroid. In autoimmune thyroid disease it can lower the antibodies and the inflammation driving the attack. The old fear was based on incomplete lab numbers, not outcomes.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
In the mid-1990s, researchers at the Minneapolis VA Medical Center set out to study what happens when people lose weight very fast. They randomized obese volunteers to one of two liquid diets: a near-zero-fat 520-calorie plan (<2 g fat per day) or a 900-calorie plan that included 30 g of fat, with one daily meal designed to trigger a full gallbladder contraction.
The trial barely got started. Within weeks, ultrasound showed new gallstones in 4 of the 6 people on the ultra-low-fat diet. None of the 7 people eating the modest 30 g of fat developed any. The difference was so stark (p = 0.021) that the investigators stopped the study early on ethical grounds. The low-fat diet produced only about half the normal gallbladder emptying; bile sat still, cholesterol crystallized, and stones formed before anyone had lost much weight.
This was not an isolated curiosity. Similar very-low-calorie, very-low-fat trials from the same era produced gallstones in roughly one-quarter to one-half of participants. The pattern was consistent: when dietary fat falls low enough that the gallbladder is rarely asked to squeeze, stasis plus cholesterol-rich bile becomes a perfect storm.
That finding landed in the middle of a much larger cultural experiment. From the late 1970s onward, official dietary guidelines steadily pushed the public toward lower fat intakes. Fat was framed as the primary dietary villain; grocery shelves filled with fat-free and low-fat products. Over the same decades, U.S. gallstone disease prevalence roughly doubled—from about 7.4% in the late 1980s to 13.9% by 2017–2020—while rates of gallbladder surgery rose in parallel.
The parallel is not proof of simple cause and effect. Obesity, insulin resistance, and rapid weight-loss cycles also climbed. Yet the mechanistic evidence is hard to ignore: the gallbladder is a muscle that needs periodic mechanical work. Extremely low-fat diets, whether temporary or habitual, deprive it of that work. The 1996 trial simply showed, in real time and under controlled conditions, what a population-scale reduction in dietary fat might have been doing more slowly for years.
Fat is not merely a calorie. For the gallbladder, it is the signal to empty. Remove the signal and the organ can quietly fill with stones.

virals.name: clem 🤗
virals.text:
We’re not going to win by lobbying, plotting, or manipulating. We’re going to win by building, in the open, with the whole community!

Today, with @ggerganov we’re super excited to announce the release of llama.cpp v1, the first major fully stable version of the most used library to run AI models locally, meaning on your phone, your laptop, and your workstation.

It means you can own your intelligence for free, not send your data to anyone and be 100% in control, wherever you are in the world. It shows our commitment to support every hardware, platform and model type out there and makes AI distributed rather than concentrated in a few Silicon Valley orgs.

Huge thanks to the team, the long-time maintainers and every contributor who helped make this happen. Let’s build! 💛🧡💚

virals.name: @levelsio
virals.text:
More progress!

Interior AI 3D works with "just" a floor plan now

Not much information to work with and it has to imagine furniture etc. but it works

Some weird things like the big I guess sliding windows to outdoor garden are missing, and bath tub is just a box, and I don't see a toilet seat etc. so we need it to become a bit more granular/specific/advanced

But it's very promising

It was really impossible until recently do to floor plan to 3d automatically and properly!

virals.name: @levelsio

✨ Progress update:

I imported the entire catalogue of @IKEA in 3d into Interior AI after seeing someone do the same yesterday, I'll try to import more furniture brands soon to get more variety too

And this is with lighting probes as suggested by @threejs @mrdoob

This seems way more powerful than just basic image in image out restylings
